power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Measuring Cognitive Demands in Professional Esports

author.affiliation:

text.text: Practice may improve certain cognitive skills more than others because those skills are called upon more frequently during an activity.
Professional esports provides a means of measuring these demands during gameplay because match records capture the information available to players and their responses as events unfold.
This study introduces the Telemetry and Replay Analysis of Cognitive Exposure (TRACE) framework, which measures seven dimensions of cognitive demand in professional esports.
The analysis used records from 314 professional DOTA 2 matches, covering 558 distinct player accounts and approximately 2,184 player-hours of competition.

TRACE defines four measures at the player level (cognitive control capacity, task switching, inhibitory control, and dynamic attention) and three measures at the team level (visuospatial working memory and updating, decision-making under uncertainty, and feedback learning).
Hierarchical Bayesian models estimated each dimension in its original units and on a common percentile scale, accounting for differences among teams, matches, and hero-role combinations.
By identifying comparable situations across matches, TRACE can quantify how often players encounter a given demand and how they respond when it arises.
This transforms routinely recorded match replays into a source of large-scale behavioral data for cognitive psychology.
The cognitive benefits of video game training vary depending on the game played, even when training time is held constant.
After 20 hours of practice, for example, the action-game group became more accurate at detecting changes in object orientation.
Meanwhile, the hidden-object group searched faster and recalled locations more accurately (Oei & Patterson, 2013).
text.formatted: Meanwhile, the hidden-object group searched faster and recalled locations more accurately <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Oei & Patterson, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Action game training has been shown to improve visual attention (Bediou et al., 2023; Green & Bavelier, 2003 , 2006), and older adults have demonstrated improvements in working memory after playing strategy or multitasking games (Anguera et al., 2013; Basak et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Action game training has been shown to improve visual attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bediou et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Green & Bavelier, 2003</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">, 2006)</ref>, and older adults have demonstrated improvements in working memory after playing strategy or multitasking games <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anguera et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Basak et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Participants who managed two bases in a strategy game demonstrated greater improvements in cognitive flexibility than participants who played a life simulation game (Glass et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Participants who managed two bases in a strategy game demonstrated greater improvements in cognitive flexibility than participants who played a life simulation game <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Glass et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These differences may reflect how frequently each game engages particular cognitive skills (Dale et al., 2020; Oei & Patterson, 2013 , 2015).
text.formatted: These differences may reflect how frequently each game engages particular cognitive skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dale et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Oei & Patterson, 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Within a single game, the demands on attention, memory, and decision-making can vary from one situation to the next.
In the same visual environment, a change in the immediate goal redirects where people look (Rothkopf et al., 2007; Sullivan et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In the same visual environment, a change in the immediate goal redirects where people look <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rothkopf et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Sullivan et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: When sorting objects, people retain features relevant to the next step and rely more on memory if they can anticipate which feature they will need (Droll & Hayhoe, 2007; Droll et al., 2005).
text.formatted: When sorting objects, people retain features relevant to the next step and rely more on memory if they can anticipate which feature they will need <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Droll & Hayhoe, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Droll et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, what people learn from an outcome depends on whether they expect earlier experience to be useful (Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Similarly, what people learn from an outcome depends on whether they expect earlier experience to be useful <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Behrens et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Nassar et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Linking players' actions to the available information at the time would demonstrate how frequently particular demands arise during practice and how players respond to them.

Professional DOTA 2 play requires split-second decisions and long-term planning under incomplete information (OpenAI et al., 2019), making it ideal for studying how cognitive demands change during play.
text.formatted: Professional DOTA 2 play requires split-second decisions and long-term planning under incomplete information <ref type="bibr">(OpenAI et al., 2019)</ref>, making it ideal for studying how cognitive demands change during play.

text.text: For example, consider a team deciding whether to start a fight.
An opponent visible on the far side of the map poses a different decision problem than an opponent last seen there a minute ago.
The opponent may be in the same place in both cases, but the team must act with greater uncertainty in the second case.

Match replays make this distinction observable, as researchers can use recorded events to reconstruct player movements and identify encounters between opponents (Drachen et al., 2014; Schubert et al., 2016), as well as determine which opponents were visible to each team at the time (Carvalho et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Match replays make this distinction observable, as researchers can use recorded events to reconstruct player movements and identify encounters between opponents <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Drachen et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Schubert et al., 2016)</ref>, as well as determine which opponents were visible to each team at the time <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Carvalho et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Ma et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: framework, which measures seven dimensions of cognitive demand at the player and team levels.
For each dimension, TRACE defines a recurring situation in terms of observable match events and specifies which aspects can be measured when that situation occurs.
Some measures describe the information available to players, while others describe how often players act or the outcomes teams achieve under specific conditions.
Hierarchical Bayesian models estimate each measure in its original units and place it on a common percentile scale.
Together, these measures transform routine match records into large-scale behavioral data on the cognitive demands that players encounter and how they respond during competition.
Records from 314 professional DOTA 2 matches covered 558 distinct player accounts and approximately 2,184 player-hours of competition.
One hundred and fourteen of these matches were played by 80 players from 16 teams at PGL Wallachia Season 9 under game version 7.41f.
This tournament served as the basis for comparing cognitive demands.
The remaining 200 matches were sampled by tournament and date from the two preceding game versions (100 from each of versions 7.41d and 7.41e).
These matches contributed to the estimation of six of the seven measures; dynamic attention was estimated using only the 114 matches from version 7.41f (Supplementary Table S1).
text.formatted: These matches contributed to the estimation of six of the seven measures; dynamic attention was estimated using only the 114 matches from version 7.41f (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: OpenDota match records identified each player's hero, or the character controlled by the player, and provided an estimate of their role on the team.
The five roles are numbered from 1 to 5, in order of typical priority for in-game resources: carry, mid laner, offlaner, soft support, and hard support, respectively.
PGL Wallachia Season 9 included 141 unique hero-role combinations.
Match records also provided team lineups, fights, kills, and gold gains.
Replays supplied player locations, team visibility, health, ability use, and combat events.
The two sources were linked by match ID and elapsed game time.
Table 1 pairs each cognitive dimension with the corresponding measurement event.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref> pairs each cognitive dimension with the corresponding measurement event.

text.text: The distinction between updating, switching, and inhibition is based on the work of Miyake et al. (2000).
text.formatted: The distinction between updating, switching, and inhibition is based on the work of <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Miyake et al. (2000)</ref>.

text.text: The measure of visuospatial working memory and updating is based on the role of working memory in retaining and using information (Baddeley, 1992).
text.formatted: The measure of visuospatial working memory and updating is based on the role of working memory in retaining and using information <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baddeley, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Four measures describe an individual player during a match.
The other three measures use information or outcomes shared by a team and provide one observation per team per match.
Each measure has its own observation time or set of eligible events.
Events with missing required game states were excluded.
A measure was missing for a player or team with no eligible events.
Information measures use base-two logarithms and are expressed in bits (Shannon, 1948).
text.formatted: Information measures use base-two logarithms and are expressed in bits <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Shannon, 1948)</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary Table S2 provides the event rules and reference distributions.
text.formatted: Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S2</ref> provides the event rules and reference distributions.

text.text: Location information gain, peripheral cue information, and feedback information gain share a calculation.
Each one compares the two probabilities assigned to the actual outcome.
The mean gain in bits per scored event is G= 1 where N is the number of scored events for the player or team in that match and i indexes those events.
For event i, p i is the probability of the observed outcome given the additional information, and q i is its probability under the baseline for that measure.
A positive value of G means that, on average on the log scale, the additional information improved prediction of the observed outcomes.
As a player moves through the map, nearby ability casts, item uses, abrupt health losses, control onsets, and changes in hero visibility alter the stream of information available to them.
The visible event information rate measures how much information this stream carries per second.
Events visible within 1,600 game units were counted in 0.5-second bins.
A Poisson reference model was used to estimate the probability of each channel count, taking into account the game version, hero, and game phase.
Rolespecific rates were adjusted toward that baseline.
The sum of the negative log probabilities across channels and bins (including empty bins) was divided by the player's observed time in seconds.
Even when an opponent disappears from a team's view, its last known position can still help predict where it will reappear.
Location information gain measures the contribution of that prior spatial information.

For each reappearance, the location distribution based on the last visible coordinates, time out of sight, and base movement speed was compared to the distribution of map locations within the same game version.
The use of teleport mixed the map distribution into the conditional prediction.
The two probabilities were evaluated at the cell where the opponent reappeared and scored for the observing team.
After a player leaves one lane for another, their opponents may approach the location that they just left.
Risk-conditioned switching measures the proportion of confirmed lane switches that are followed by a specified risk at the original location.
A switch requires the use of a teleport scroll or Twin Gate after minute 10, as well as displacement of at least 3,000 game units between lanes.
The origin was checked at 3, 7, 12, and 20 seconds after the switch.
The risk condition required at least two living enemies within 1,800 units or one living enemy with cumulative gold at least 1.25 times the player's.
All confirmed switches for that player in the match formed the denominator.
The appearance of a new opponent during an attack gives the player an opportunity to stop attacking and withdraw.

An opportunity becomes eligible when a player with at least 60% health attacks a visible enemy within 1,600 game units and a second enemy appears 1-5 seconds later, having been unseen for the preceding 5 seconds.
To disengage, the player must move at least 500 units away from the original target within eight seconds of the new arrival.
They must also refrain from attacking enemy heroes and survive for 15 seconds.
Disengagement probability uses all eligible opportunities for that player in the match as its denominator.
While a player is securing a last hit, an enemy appearing on the periphery can alert them to potential danger.
A peripheral cue is an enemy that has been unseen for five seconds and appears one to five seconds after the last hit, at a distance of 1,200 to 2,200 game units.
In both cue and no-cue contexts, the outcome was whether the player died within 25 s after the last hit.
This comparison accounted for health, game phase, and nearby visible enemies.
The peripheral cue information compared the probability of the observed outcome with and without the cue, scoring only eligible cue contexts for that player.
A team may initiate a fight when the locations of the key opponents are unknown.
One second before initiation, the two living opponents with the most cumulative gold were identified.
Initiations were classified as "informed" when both opponents were visible to the initiating team and "uncertain" when at least one opponent was unseen.
An initiation was considered profitable if the initiating team gained more gold than the opposing team during the fight.
The initiation profit ratio was calculated by dividing the estimated probability of a profitable outcome under uncertainty by the corresponding probability when informed.
The two estimates used separate counts of profitable and eligible initiations for each team.
After a team loses a hero in a fight, the role of the first hero lost can inform predictions about later fights.
Feedback information gain compares a prediction based on earlier first losses in that match with a baseline estimated from other matches in the same game version.

Before each eligible fight, the updated probability is p t ( r )= 30 p 0 ( r )+ n r , t -1 30+ N t -1 , where t indexes eligible fights for the defending team in that match and r denotes a role. p 0 ( r ) is the baseline probability that the first hero lost plays that role.

The constant 30 gives the baseline the weight of 30 prior observations. n r , t -1 counts earlier eligible fights in which the first hero lost played role r, and N t -1 counts all earlier eligible fights for that team.
The first fight initialized the counts.
For each subsequent fight, p t ( r ) and p 0 ( r ) were evaluated at the role actually lost before that fight was added to the counts.
Corpus summaries used all eligible observations for each dimension (see Table 2).
text.formatted: Corpus summaries used all eligible observations for each dimension (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref>).

text.text: First, continuous measures were calculated for each player or team in each match.
The reported mean and sample standard deviation give these observations equal weight.
For task switching and inhibitory control, the overall proportions are calculated by dividing the total number of qualifying responses or outcomes by the total number of eligible opportunities.
For decision-making under uncertainty, the proportion of profitable initiations was calculated separately for each information condition and then divided (uncertain versus informed).
A separate hierarchical Bayesian model was used to estimate each of the seven dimensions defined in Table 1.
text.formatted: A separate hierarchical Bayesian model was used to estimate each of the seven dimensions defined in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: The models for cognitive control capacity, task switching, inhibitory control, and dynamic attention used one observation per eligible player per match.
For the dimensions of visuospatial working memory and updating, decision-making under uncertainty, and feedback learning, each eligible team contributed one observation per match.
All models included effects for team, match, and hero-role combination.
The four player-level models also included player and role effects.
For team-level outcomes, the model averaged the hero-role effects of the five players in the lineup.
Gaussian random walks allowed the overall level and the hero-role effects to vary across successive game versions.
For cognitive control capacity, the observed information rate was divided by its median, then fitted with a gamma likelihood and log link.
The shape parameter was proportional to the match duration, which gave longer observations greater precision at the same expected rate.
For visuospatial working memory and updating, dynamic attention, and feedback learning, the observed quantity was the average information gain across eligible events in a match.
Each measure was centered at its median and divided by its standard deviation before fitting.
The model for visuospatial working memory and updating employed a Student's t-distribution with four fixed degrees of freedom.
This specification gives extreme observations less influence on the estimated mean than a normal likelihood does, retains finite variance, and requires no separate estimate of tail thickness.
For dynamic attention and feedback learning, a mixture of two normal distributions accommodated occasional high values while preserving the predicted mean.
In all three models, the base residual scale decreased as the number of eligible events increased (see Supplementary Table S3).
text.formatted: In all three models, the base residual scale decreased as the number of eligible events increased (see Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: For task switching, the numerator was the number of lane switches followed by risk at the original location.
The denominator was the total number of confirmed switches.
For inhibitory control, the numerator was the number of withdrawals, while the denominator was all eligible new threat opportunities.
Beta-binomial likelihoods retained these denominators and permitted response probabilities to fluctuate beyond the scope of ordinary binomial variation.

For decision-making under uncertainty, two beta-binomial components estimated the probability of profitable initiation under uncertain and informed conditions; each component used its own eligible initiations.
The reported probability ratio was obtained by dividing the former probability by the latter.
Supplementary Table S4 reports sampling diagnostics and posterior predictive checks.
text.formatted: Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S4</ref> reports sampling diagnostics and posterior predictive checks.

text.text: To decide whether to include earlier game versions, two models were fitted to the first 25 matches of version 7.41f for each dimension: one with the 200 matches from the two earlier versions and one without.
Then, predictive log densities were compared on the remaining 89 matches.
The earlier versions were retained if the upper bound of the 95% match-bootstrap interval for the mean difference (with and without the earlier versions) was at least zero.
This rule retained the earlier versions for six dimensions.
The final dynamic attention model used the 114 matches from version 7.41f.
For the four dimensions measured in bits per event or bits per second, reference probabilities were calculated from other matches across the full window for each game version.
The comparison for these dimensions was conditional on those reference probabilities (see Supplementary Table S5).
text.formatted: The comparison for these dimensions was conditional on those reference probabilities (see Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: In version 7.41f, estimates for each hero-role combination set team, match, and player effects to zero, where applicable.
For team-level dimensions, the estimates are averaged over observed lineups containing that combination.
Player and team profiles retained the contexts in which they actually competed.
Within each posterior draw, the estimates were weighted by match duration for cognitive control capacity and by eligible event counts for the other dimensions.
For decision-making under uncertainty, the two probabilities of profitable initiation were aggregated separately before taking their ratio (see Supplementary Table S3).

text.text: The reference consisted of the 141 hero-role combinations observed in version 7.41f, each of which was given equal weight.
Within each joint posterior draw, the percentile was defined as the percentage of reference estimates that fell below the estimate of interest.
Ties were assigned half weight.
The reported percentile is the mean of these draw-level percentiles.
Estimates in the original units are posterior medians.
For each scale, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the posterior draws define the 95% posterior interval.
To summarize the variation among the reference values, the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the 141 modeled values were calculated in their original units within each posterior draw.
Each quartile is reported as the median across draws, with a 95% posterior interval.
This summary includes all 141 combinations, even those for which an estimate depended on the hierarchical model because the combination had no eligible events in the target version.
The models were fitted in PyMC 5.28.5 (Abril-Pla et al., 2023) using the No-U-Turn sampler (Hoffman & Gelman, 2014) in nutpie 0.16.11.
text.formatted: The models were fitted in PyMC 5.28.5 <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abril-Pla et al., 2023)</ref> using the No-U-Turn sampler <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hoffman & Gelman, 2014)</ref> in nutpie 0.16.11.

text.text: Each of the four chains underwent 2,500 warm-up iterations, followed by 4,000 retained draws, targeting a .995 acceptance probability.
ArviZ 0.23.4 (Kumar et al., 2019) provided the rank-normalized R-hat statistic and the bulk and tail effective sample sizes (Vehtari et al., 2021).
text.formatted: ArviZ 0.23.4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Kumar et al., 2019)</ref> provided the rank-normalized R-hat statistic and the bulk and tail effective sample sizes <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Vehtari et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The study required a maximum R-hat of 1.01 or lower and minimum bulk and tail effective sample sizes of 400 or higher with zero divergent transitions.
Posterior predictive checks compared the fitted observations with replicated data drawn from the posterior predictive distribution (Gelman et al., 1996).
text.formatted: Posterior predictive checks compared the fitted observations with replicated data drawn from the posterior predictive distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Gelman et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Two sets of counts were contributed to decisionmaking under uncertainty: one for informed initiations and one for uncertain initiations.
This yielded eight observed outcomes across the seven models.
For each outcome, the observed mean was compared with the central 95% interval of simulated means.
The second check required that at least 90% of the observations fall within their respective 95% posterior predictive intervals.
Both checks used the scale on which the outcome was fitted, including event counts for the beta-binomial models (see Supplementary Table S4).
text.formatted: Both checks used the scale on which the outcome was fitted, including event counts for the beta-binomial models (see Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: For cognitive control capacity, visible events carried an average of 4.01 bits/s (SD = 0.65) across 3,140 player-match observations (Figure 1).
text.formatted: For cognitive control capacity, visible events carried an average of 4.01 bits/s (SD = 0.65) across 3,140 player-match observations (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: For task switching, the original location met the risk criterion after 719 out of 6,450 confirmed lane switches (11.1%).
For inhibitory control, players withdrew on 3,182 out of 16,673 eligible occasions when a new opponent appeared during an attack (19.1%).

For dynamic attention, the information that a peripheral cue provided about subsequent death or survival averaged 0.063 bits per cue context (SD = 0.321) across 1,001 player-match observations in version 7.41f.
Table 2 provides the sample size and denominator for each dimension.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref> provides the sample size and denominator for each dimension.

text.text: For visuospatial working memory and updating, the average location information gain was 2.61 bits per reappearance (SD = 0.25) across 628 team-match observations.
This gain describes the improvement in predicting where an opponent would reappear based on the last known position and time out of view.

Regarding decision-making under uncertainty, 570 out of 1,071 initiations were profitable when at least one of the two highest-gold living opponents was out of view (53.2%), compared to 159 out of 315 when both were visible (50.5%).
The observed probability ratio was 1.05.

For feedback learning, using earlier fights to predict the role of the first hero lost by the defending team in the next fight yielded a mean gain of 0.0064 bits per feedback event (SD = 0.0739) across 581 team-match observations.
Version 7.41f included 114 matches, 80 players, 16 teams, and 141 unique hero-role combinations.
The middle half of the modeled values for cognitive control capacity across these combinations ranged from 3.67 to 4.03 bits/s.
For inhibitory control, the corresponding range was .160 to .226 for the probability of withdrawal when a new opponent appeared.
Figure 2 shows the three quartiles and their 95% posterior intervals in the original units for each dimension.

text.text: For decision-making under uncertainty, the median ratio of profitable initiation probabilities across these combinations was 1.05 (95% posterior interval [0.92, 1.23]).
The estimated 25th and 75th percentiles were 1.00 and 1.11, respectively.
A ratio of 1 indicates the same probability of profitable initiation under uncertain and informed conditions.

text.text: Decisionmaking under uncertainty provided separate counts of profitable initiations under informed and uncertain conditions, resulting in eight observed mean outcomes across the seven models.
Checks on the fitted data revealed that all eight observed means fell within the corresponding 95% intervals for means from posterior predictive replicates.
Across the eight outcomes, 96.9%-100% of observations fell within their respective 95% posterior predictive intervals.
All seven models met the sampling criteria (see Supplementary Table S4).

text.text: The match records revealed the available information during play, how frequently players performed a specific action when the opportunity arose, and the outcomes teams achieved under various information conditions.
Estimated profiles varied across hero-role combinations within a single game version, demonstrating that players competing under the same rules experienced different patterns of demand.
doing and what information was available at the time.
Inhibitory control is one example.
When a previously unseen opponent appeared during an attack, the player had the opportunity to stop an action that was already in progress.
Players stopped attacking and withdrew on 3,182 of the 16,673 eligible occasions (19.1%).
text.formatted: Players stopped attacking and withdrew on 3,182 of the 16,673 eligible occasions <ref type="bibr">(19.1%)</ref>.

text.text: Distinguishing between occasions when players encountered a new threat and occasions when they withdrew when one appeared is important.
Task context plays a similar role in studies of visual attention, in which people look at different objects in the same visual environment depending on their immediate goal (Rothkopf et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Task context plays a similar role in studies of visual attention, in which people look at different objects in the same visual environment depending on their immediate goal <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rothkopf et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Differences in cognitive demands within the same game enable researchers to compare the opportunities players have to practice under the same rules and with the same objective.
In DOTA 2, for example, estimated demand profiles varied across hero-role combinations within the same game version (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: In DOTA 2, for example, estimated demand profiles varied across hero-role combinations within the same game version (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Therefore, two players could spend the same amount of time in DOTA 2 yet face different decisions repeatedly.
This distinction is important when a study uses playing time to determine how much practice participants have received.
An hour in which a particular decision arises repeatedly and an hour in which it never arises count equally toward total playing time.
By counting the number of times each participant faced a particular decision, researchers can compare how much opportunity each participant had to practice making that decision.

The extent to which practice in a game transfers to an untrained task may depend on how closely the cognitive demands of the two activities align. Oei and Patterson (2015) classified four action games according to their perceptual and attentional demands.
text.formatted: The extent to which practice in a game transfers to an untrained task may depend on how closely the cognitive demands of the two activities align. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Oei and Patterson (2015)</ref> classified four action games according to their perceptual and attentional demands.

text.text: They then examined how performance on related tasks changed after 20 hours of training.
Participants who trained on the game requiring the fastest shifts of attention improved at detecting a second target presented shortly after the first.
A DOTA 2 study could use TRACE profiles to select practice tasks that differ in visible event information rate.
Players would be randomly assigned to these tasks for the same number of hours, and their replays would provide an estimate of the actual information rate encountered by each player.

Then, an independent test of cognitive control capacity, administered before and after training, could establish whether higher information rates during practice predict greater improvement on the test.
The reference distribution is based on 114 professional matches played in version 7.41f.
Players with different skill levels or playing other versions of the game may encounter different situations or respond to them differently.
Therefore, the same measured value could correspond to a different percentile in those settings.
Additionally, the study lacked independent cognitive test scores with which to evaluate differences between players.
Three of the seven dimensions describe information or outcomes shared by a team.

To interpret differences between players as differences in ability, it would be necessary to demonstrate that the differences recur across matches and correspond to performance on independent tests of the relevant ability (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955; Hedge et al., 2018).
text.formatted: To interpret differences between players as differences in ability, it would be necessary to demonstrate that the differences recur across matches and correspond to performance on independent tests of the relevant ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cronbach & Meehl, 1955;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hedge et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Match replays preserve the information available to players when they act, enabling researchers to identify repeated decisions and examine players' responses.
These routinely recorded matches allow cognitive psychologists to study the decisions players made during many hours of competition while retaining the context of each decision.
